column1: In keyframe animation, what does a linear interpolation between two keyframes imply about velocity, and why does this look robotic?
column2: It implies constant velocity—uniform speed from start to finish. It looks robotic because real-world motion involves acceleration/deceleration from forces like gravity, friction, and inertia, which linear interpolation fails to capture.

column1: Why does human perception treat 24-60 fps as the practical range for animation frame rates?
column2: Below ~18 fps, viewers consciously perceive flicker rather than motion. Above 60 fps, perceptual gains diminish steeply, so the rendering cost of extra frames yields minimal improvement in perceived smoothness.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing hierarchical transformation inheritance in skeletal rigs?
column2: When a parent bone rotates, all descendant bones in its subtree inherit that rotation and compound it with their own local rotations to produce world-space poses—mirroring how shoulder rotation moves the elbow, wrist, and fingers.

column1: What is the architectural distinction between the control skeleton and the deformation skeleton in production rigs?
column2: The control skeleton exists for animator ergonomics (may be repositioned, scaled, or constrained for intuitive handles like foot-roll or pole vectors); the deformation skeleton is the actual joint chain that drives vertex positions via skinning weights. They are kept separate to allow sophisticated controls without affecting deformation directly.

column1: What differential continuity condition must believable animated motion satisfy, and when is it deliberately violated?
column2: Motion must exhibit continuous second-order differentiability (smooth acceleration) except at deliberate impact events; discontinuous acceleration implies physically impossible teleportation of energy, while discontinuous velocity signals collision or constraint satisfaction.

column1: How do the animation principles of 'timing' and 'spacing' map to physical quantities?
column2: Timing (number of frames allocated to an action) controls velocity magnitude; spacing (distribution of inbetween positions) defines the acceleration profile through implicit differentiation.

column1: What physical law do anticipation and follow-through express in animation?
column2: Newton's third law: preparatory countermotion precedes the primary action (anticipation), and momentum dissipates gradually rather than instantaneously (follow-through).

column1: What invariant underlies squash and stretch deformation?
column2: Energy and volume conservation during elastic deformation—reciprocal scaling along orthogonal axes preserves volume as the object compresses in one axis and expands in another.

column1: What is the core tradeoff between destructive and non-destructive animation workflows?
column2: Destructive workflows bake calculations permanently, collapsing the dependency stack and losing the ability to iterate upstream, but save memory/evaluation time. Non-destructive workflows preserve the full transformation chain (modifier stacks, procedural systems) for flexibility at the cost of memory overhead and evaluation time.

column1: What is the hard temporal budget per frame for real-time animation evaluation at 24-60 fps?
column2: 16 to 41 milliseconds per frame—every deformation calculation, physics step, and shader evaluation must complete within this window.

column1: Describe the memory hierarchy flow for high-resolution geometry in a 3D animation pipeline.
column2: Static mesh data lives in permanent storage, is loaded into system RAM during scene initialization, then transferred to GPU VRAM for rasterization; deformation data (blend shapes, bone transforms, cloth states) occupies intermediate cache layers with refresh strategy depending on keyframed vs. procedural animation.

column1: Why is a parametric curve (time normalized to [0,1]) the mathematical foundation of temporal geometry rather than describing y as a function of x?
column2: Because animation requires describing position/rotation as a function of a single time parameter mapped to 3D values, allowing a unified framework for interpolating state across frames rather than a direct geometric function of spatial coordinates.
